sections.h2: Your three ways to sell in Georgetown
sections.html:
Three paths exist here: accept a cash bid, hire an agent to list, or find a buyer yourself. Cash gives the fastest, surest finish. A listing reaches the most eyes. Going alone saves the most in fees.

Georgetown seats Williamson County and ranks among the quickest-growing U.S. cities over 50,000 people. Residents numbered 47,400 in 2010 and 67,176 in 2020, and the mid-2025 estimate stands at 106,907. Demand is steady, yet a resale shares the market with plenty of new construction. Investors name a price and a day with no open houses, while a listing suits people who want a polished, staged home to show.

  • Cash bid: sold as-is, closing on your schedule, almost no prep.
  • Agent listing: more exposure, more effort, and repair asks once the inspector visits.
  • Do it yourself: cheapest, though contracts and buyer vetting land on you.

Most Georgetown homes are owner-occupied, and the middle value is $429,100. Think of these figures as backdrop for your own estimate, not a price tag on your house.

Georgetown housing, 2020 to 2024 survey

Owing money on the house? Ask your servicer for a payoff quote before anything else, because no offer can sensibly fall under it. Plenty of longtime owners in town are older and thinking about a smaller place, a move nearer relatives or an estate to wrap up, and each of those tends to favor a simple, fast sale.

If your house stands in or near the older blocks around the Square, expect some extra questions. The town counts four National Register historic districts and 52 individually listed properties.

Buyers who love character homes and walkable streets gravitate there. Landmarks close by include the Public Square, the 1911 Williamson County Courthouse, Southwestern University, Lake Georgetown and the San Gabriel River trails.

  • Call the planning office to learn whether your lot falls within a historic district or carries design standards.
  • Mention any permitted exterior projects to buyers at the start.
  • An investor can take an older house as it stands, skipping the punch list a retail buyer may write.

People recognize the Square's shops and restaurants and the 1911 courthouse. Trails matter too: nearly nine miles of hike and bike paths along the San Gabriel River, nearly seven miles in Garey Park, and 28 miles around Lake Georgetown.

Living near one of these is worth stating directly, whether you list or talk to a cash buyer, since location feeds the price. Measure distances yourself. Make no promises about school zoning or future building, and send buyers to the school district and the planning office for current boundaries and plans.

sections.h2: Property tax breaks for older and disabled owners
sections.html:
Plenty of Georgetown owners are 65 or older, so these exemptions matter. A school district must exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value, plus another $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners.

Those owners also get a ceiling on school tax for the homestead, generally frozen at the amount from the first year they qualified. Part of that ceiling can travel to a new Texas homestead, scaled to the new house, though additions beyond ordinary repairs can raise it. A surviving spouse aged 55 or older sometimes keeps it. Cities, counties and junior college districts may set ceilings of their own.

Owners with a service-connected disability rating qualify for separate exemptions, from up to $5,000 at a 10 to 29 percent rating to up to $12,000 at 70 to 100 percent. A homestead owner rated 100 percent disabled gets a full exemption. Ask the Williamson County appraisal district which ones you hold and how moving would change your ceiling.

Everything follows the statewide calendar. Values lock on January 1, and bills show up around the start of October.

  • Homestead value notices start near April 1.
  • The protest window usually ends in mid-May, or 30 days after your notice if that is later.
  • Split payments: half by November 30, the remainder by June 30.
  • Anything unpaid after January 31 draws late charges.

You can carry a dispute beyond the review board into district court or binding arbitration, and to the State Office of Administrative Hearings when the value tops $1,000,000. Pay the undisputed share before the delinquency date while you appeal.

Missing documents slow closings more often than repairs do. A tidy folder lets you weigh bids side by side and gives the title company less to chase after you say yes.

  • Your latest tax statement, naming each taxing unit.
  • Payoff letters for every loan, second mortgages and equity lines included.
  • Proof of any homestead, senior or disability exemption.
  • Permits and receipts for earlier work, especially near the older neighborhoods.
  • Signatures from co-owners or heirs.

Then ask a cash buyer for a written bid stating price and closing day, and ask an agent for a range based on nearby sales. Judge each by what lands in your pocket after payoffs and closing charges, not by the top-line number. The title company can draft a one-page net sheet that lines them up.

A cash buyer needs no lender appraisal or loan approval, so those weeks vanish. Title work stays: the title company searches the record, gathers payoff letters, drafts the deed and a settlement statement, and holds funds until every signature is in.

Ask the buyer how long the search will take and whether you pick the date. Need a few extra days to move out? Get a short post-closing stay in writing. Read the settlement statement the day before, so any charge you do not recognize gets raised while it is still easy to fix. If a buyer asks for a repair credit late in the process, compare it with what an as-is price already reflects before you agree.

You can sell once ownership is on paper. An heir missing from the recorded deed who wants the homestead exemption has to hand the appraisal district an affidavit of interest, a death certificate and a utility bill.

Property covered by a recorded transfer on death deed bypasses probate. Probate filings, small estate affidavits and deed recordings all go through the county clerk. Before meeting buyers, round up the death certificate, any will and the lenders' payoff statements.

On closing day the title company confirms who is allowed to sign, pays off liens from the proceeds and files the deed. A buyer who takes the house as-is saves heirs the cleanout, the repairs and months of carrying costs.

faqs.q: Does Georgetown's growth help a quick sale?
faqs.a: Fast growth supports demand, with 106,907 residents estimated for 2025. Your own price and condition set the pace, so weigh offers by net proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the middle home value in Georgetown?
faqs.a: The survey puts it at $429,100 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. Use it as background only.

faqs.q: Can seniors take their school tax ceiling to a new home?
faqs.a: Yes, in proportion, if you buy another Texas homestead. Check with the appraisal district first.

faqs.q: Which county records my Georgetown deed?
faqs.a: Williamson County, which has its seat at Georgetown. Deeds are filed with that county's clerk.

faqs.q: Do historic rules reach a newer Georgetown house?
faqs.a: Only if your address falls inside a district. Ask the city planning office, and keep permit records for any exterior work.
